engine](#-the-ranking-engine-random-walk-with-restart) - [The Model jury on Snowflake Cortex](#-the-model-jury-on-snowflake-cortex) - [Results](#-results) - [Data](#-data) - [Run it](#-run-it) - [Repository map](#-repository-map) ## 🔬 How it works ![Half Life workflow: connect biology, rank medicines, trace evidence, three AI reviews, compare rankings, save, and an optional 3D pose](docs/images/workflow.png) The ranking comes from biomedical data and graph algorithms, not from an AI model. The AI only reviews the shortlist. 1. **Connect.** Open Targets gives the proteins linked to the disease, ChEMBL gives each drug's proteins, and both are placed on STRING 12.5's network of human protein interactions. 2. **Rank and shortlist.** A random walk scores every drug. The top 10 by network plus the top 5 by direct evidence make 15 Candidates, each with the protein paths that link it to the disease. 3. **Review.** Three AI models read the same cited evidence, blind to the scores, and vote. 4. **Dock, on request.** For a drug and protein with a known 3D structure, AutoDock Vina predicts how the drug might sit in the protein. It shows a possible fit, not that the drug works, and it doesn't change the ranking. ## 🧭 The ranking engine: random walk with restart Picture a walker on the protein network. It starts on the disease's proteins and keeps stepping to random neighbours. At every step it has a 30% chance of jumping back to a disease protein. After many steps, proteins near the disease get visited often; distant ones rarely. A drug scores high when its target proteins get visited a lot. ![Random walk with restart on a toy protein network](docs/images/rwr-walk.gif) The red dot is the walker. Glow shows how often each protein is visited. Drug B's target is one step from a disease protein, so it's visited most; Drug C is far away and scores lowest. Unlike a single shortest path, the walk counts every route between a drug and the disease. The shortest paths from each drug's targets to the disease's proteins are saved as its explanation. The maths, settings and test results are in [`docs/method/ranking/RWR.md`](docs/method/ranking/RWR.md). ## 🤖 The Model jury on Snowflake Cortex The jury is three models (GPT-5.4, GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3) running on Snowflake Cortex, Snowflake's hosted AI service. Each one ranks the shortlist from the same evidence packets, without seeing the network scores. Every reply is checked before it counts: - it must be valid JSON and rank every Candidate exactly once; - it may cite only real evidence IDs; - it must quote numbers exactly as the evidence states them. Failed or refused replies are recorded, never filled in. Votes are combined by Borda count over the valid jurors, and a consensus needs at least two. ![Model jury checks and Borda count](docs/images/jury-checks.gif) ## 📊 Results To check the method works, we hide what we already know. For each disease we take the drugs regulators have already approved for it and see whether the method ranks them near the top without being told. Rules, seeds and inputs were frozen before each test ran. Full protocols are in [`results/`](results/).
1. Network shortlist: random walk finds 15 of 293 approved drugs across 14 diseases
Each method picks 15 of 1,956 drugs per disease. We count how many drugs already approved for that disease made the 15 (293 possible). Higher is better. | | Random choice | Z-score | Random walk | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Approved drugs found | about 2 | 11 | **15** | | Recall (macro) | 0.8% | 5.1% | **6.9%** | Both methods find 5-7 times more approved drugs than random choice, so the protein network carries real signal. Random walk did slightly better than z-score.
2. Model jury: blind test on 14 new diseases, drug names hidden, pre-registered
Each panel has 15 drugs: 1 already approved for the disease and 14 that aren't. The model ranks them without seeing drug names. Hits@5 counts how often the approved drug lands in the top 5 (chance 33%); MRR rewards ranking it higher (chance 0.22, perfect 1.0). The p-value is the chance a score this high happens by luck; below 0.05 means it beat chance. | Method | Hits@5 | MRR | Beats chance? (p) | |---|---:|---:|---| | GPT-5.4 alone | 8 / 14 | **0.461** | **Yes** (0.013) | | Claude Opus 5.5 alone | 6 / 14 | **0.422** | **Yes** (0.049) | | Kimi K3 alone | 7 / 14 | 0.374 | No (0.19) | | Three-model jury | 4 / 14 | 0.210 | No | | Direct-evidence ranking | 0 / 14 | 0.111 | No | | Network z-score | 3 / 14 | 0.182 | No | The jury lost because Opus's safety filter refused about half its calls, and a jury then only counted with all three votes. We changed the rule to use every valid juror (at least two) and replaced Opus with GLM-5.3. The new jury (GPT-5.4, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3) was chosen on separate pilot diseases and hasn't been through a full blind test yet. With drug names shown, models score much higher (MRR about 0.5-0.6 in our pilot) because they recognise the drugs. That's why the tests hide names.
3. Coverage: 1,307 of 1,956 drugs can be scored on the network
- 1,307 of 1,956 drugs (66.8%) can be scored on the protein network. - The rest: 557 have no known targets, 16 have targets not in the network, and 76 have targets outside its largest connected part. They get no network score (never zero), but can still enter through direct evidence.
## 🧬 Data | Source | Used for | |---|---| | [Open Targets](https://platform.opentargets.org/) 26.09 | Disease-protein links | | [ChEMBL](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/) 37 | Drugs and their proteins | | [STRING](https://string-db.org/) 12.5 | Protein interactions | | [Reactome](https://reactome.org/) | Pathways | | [RCSB PDB](https://www.rcsb.org/) | Protein structures for docking | | FDA, EMA, PMDA, DailyMed | Approvals and safety warnings | Large downloads stay out of Git. Each source keeps its own licence. ## 🚀 Run it Run the app locally on saved sample data, with no accounts or keys: ```bash uv sync --all-packages uv run uvicorn oxhack_api.app:app --reload # API on http://127.0.0.1:8000 cd app/web && npm install && npm run dev # website, proxies /api to the API ``` Live data, the Snowflake jury and real docking are switched on with `OXHACK_*` settings; every one is listed in [`.env.example`](.env.example) and [`app/api/README.md`](app/api/README.md). Run the tests: ```bash uv run pytest # pipeline, jury and ranking (cd app/api && uv run pytest) # API cd app/web && npm test && npm run e2e # website ``` --- tree --- .agents .claude .devcontainer .env.example .gitattributes .github .gitignore .trail AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md README.md app core deploy docs pyproject.toml results tests uv.lock

# Drug Repurposing for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Computational Docking and Literature Review Study

*February 14, 2026*

---

## Abstract

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the predominant form of pancreatic cancer, characterized by aggressive progression, late-stage diagnosis, and a dismal 5-year survival rate of approximately 7.7–10%, driven by dense desmoplastic stroma, tumor microenvironment heterogeneity, and dominant oncogenic drivers such as KRAS mutations in over 90% of cases. Despite advances in surgical resection and chemotherapy like gemcitabine-based regimens, unmet needs persist for targeted therapies addressing key molecular nodes including KRAS (e.g., G12D variant, PDB: 9IAY) and downstream effectors like extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 (ERK2, PDB: 2FMA), which mediate proliferation, invasion, and therapy resistance via MAPK signaling and stromal remodeling. This study integrated a comprehensive literature review of PDAC epidemiology, genetic landscape, and therapeutic targets with computational drug repurposing via DiffDock, a diffusion-based deep learning docking model executed on RunPod serverless GPU instances for efficient, parallelized virtual screening of 70 ligands against KRAS and ERK2. The review confirmed KRAS and ERK2 as preeminent targets, enriched in pathways like PI3K-Akt, focal adhesion, and ECM interactions, alongside hub genes from differentially expressed analyses. DiffDock simulations generated ranked binding poses, prioritizing FDA-approved or clinical-stage candidates; top repurposing hits included TH-Z835 (confidence 0.3483 to KRAS), BI-3406 (0.3181 to KRAS), divarasib (0.2927 to KRAS), MRTX1133 (0.2454 to KRAS), and trametinib (0.21 to ERK2), predominantly KRAS inhibitors with class expansion potential and high predicted binding reliability. These findings nominate KRAS/ERK2 modulators as promising repurposed agents to disrupt PDAC's core signaling axis, warranting experimental validation through binding assays, cell line studies, and preclinical models to confirm efficacy, selectivity, and synergy with standard therapies.

---

## 1. Introduction and Background

**Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)** is the predominant histological subtype of pancreatic cancer, characterized by aggressive biology, late-stage diagnosis, and poor prognosis.[1][2] Globally, PDAC ranks as the 14th most common malignancy, with approximately 495,773 new cases and 466,003 deaths annually, positioning it as the seventh leading cause of cancer death; incidence rates are higher in developed regions such as Europe (e.g., 9.8 per 100,000 in Western Europe for males) and North America (9.9 per 100,000 for males) compared to Africa and South Central Asia (as low as 0.46 per 100,000).[1] In the United States, age-adjusted incidence reached 13.8 new cases per 100,000 annually (2018–2022), with a death rate of 11.3 per 100,000 (2019–2023), reflecting mortality closely mirroring incidence due to advanced presentation; early-stage incidence has risen notably from 1.1 to 2.8 per 100,000 between 2001 and 2020 (annual percent change 5.7%), accompanied by improved 5-year survival for stages IA (47% to 75%) and IB (38% to 68%) from 2004 to 2015.[2][3][4]

PDAC's clinical lethality is evident in stage distributions at diagnosis—15% localized (5-year survival 43.6%), 28% regional (16.7%), and 51% distant (3.2%)—yielding an overall 5-year survival of 7.7–10% and a 1-year overall survival of 24%.[1][3] Projections indicate PDAC will become the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the US by 2030, exacerbated by desmoplastic stroma, tumor microenvironment (TME) heterogeneity, and early detection challenges; risk factors include advanced age, male sex, and regional disparities.[1][4] These trends highlight the imperative for enhanced screening, precise imaging, and therapies targeting TME-mediated invasion and resistance.[2]

#### Molecular and Genetic Landscape
PDAC's molecular hallmarks are dominated by **KRAS mutations** in over 90% of cases, particularly G12D variants that constitutively activate the protein, driving proliferation.[5] Bioinformatics of datasets (e.g., GSE28735, GSE15471, GSE62452) reveals differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in Gene Ontology and KEGG pathways related to cell proliferation, adhesion, and stromal remodeling, with hub genes and transcription factor networks delineating subtypes.[1] The TME potentiates progression via desmoplasia from cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), activating extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 (**ERK2**) in response to matrix rigidity and enabling tumor invasion; axonal remodeling and neural influences further contribute to heterogeneity, while multimodal electronic health record analyses link longitudinal patterns to KRAS-driven early detection.[1][5]

#### Therapeutic Targets and Strategies

## 3. Methodology

All molecular docking simulations were performed using DiffDock, a diffusion-based deep learning model designed for structure-based drug discovery[1]. DiffDock predicts ligand binding poses by iteratively refining ligand coordinates through a learned diffusion process, generating multiple binding poses per ligand–protein pair and ranking each pose by a confidence score ranging from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating greater predicted binding reliability. For each ligand–protein complex, ten binding poses were generated, and the pose with the highest confidence score was retained as the representative result for subsequent ranking and analysis.

### Compute Infrastructure

All docking simulations were executed on RunPod serverless GPU instances accessed via the RunPod Python SDK[1]. This cloud-based infrastructure enabled parallel GPU-accelerated inference without requiring local hardware management or maintenance. Each ligand–protein docking job was submitted to a dedicated serverless endpoint, allowing efficient batch processing and rapid turnaround of large-scale virtual screening campaigns.

### Protein Target Selection

Target proteins were selected based on their established roles in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) pathogenesis. Two primary targets were investigated: KRAS (Protein Data Bank identifier: 9IAY) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 (ERK2; PDB: 2FMA). These proteins were selected because KRAS mutations occur in approximately 90% of PDAC cases and represent a critical node in oncogenic signaling, while ERK2 functions as a key effector in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade downstream of KRAS activation. Three-dimensional protein structures were retrieved from the RCSB Protein Data Bank in standard .pdb format.

### Ligand Library Construction

Candidate compounds were retrieved from PubChem and curated drug databases, encompassing both FDA-approved pharmaceuticals and bioactive research compounds identified through target-based searches. The ligand library included direct KRAS inhibitors (sotorasib, adagrasib, divarasib, MRTX1133, RMC-4630, RMC-6236, RMC-9805, BI-3406, BI-1701963, TH-Z835), MEK/ERK pathway inhibitors (trametinib, LY3214996), compounds with indirect anti-KRAS activity (metformin, simvastatin, disulfiram, itraconazole), repurposed drugs with reported off-target MAPK inhibition (doxycycline, aspirin, thalidomide, propranolol, verapamil, cimetidine), and bioactive natural product derivatives identified through PubChem target searches.

##### pipeline.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Autonomous Drug Discovery Pipeline

Single orchestrator that runs the full pipeline: literature review →
structure retrieval → docking → **reasoning loop** → report → paper.

The reasoning loop is the agentic part: after each docking round,
Perplexity Sonar analyzes results, looks for patterns (e.g. drug-class
clustering), and decides whether to expand the search (3D similarity,
more drugs of a promising class) or proceed to synthesis.

Usage:
    python pipeline.py "pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma"
    python pipeline.py "pleural mesothelioma" --max-rounds 3
    python pipeline.py --resume   # resume from last saved state
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import re
import sys
import time
from datetime import datetime

from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Import existing pipeline functions (NO rewrites)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    search_arxiv,
    query_perplexity,
    extract_proteins_from_text,

The user's message text is treated as the cancerType.

"""

Both repos are drug repurposing projects. They take different approaches, which is useful if you're drafting a project summary. Devpost returned a 403 for Half Life, and I couldn't find a Devpost page for tree26. Everything below comes from the READMEs, the source code, and a Runpod blog post.

## tree26 / RepoRx (TreeHacks 2026, Stanford)

- **What it is:** An autonomous pipeline that takes a disease name and produces a research paper nominating existing drugs to repurpose for it. The live site is [reporx.vercel.app](https://reporx.vercel.app). The repo's own README is just "for the love of the game".
- **Result:** The [Runpod TreeHacks 2026 post](https://www.runpod.io/blog/runpod-treehacks-2026) lists RepoRx as a first-place project. It cites DiffDock docking on Runpod Serverless.
- **Pipeline:** Each step is a separate agent.
  1. **Literature review:** arXiv plus Perplexity Sonar Pro finds the disease's target proteins.
  2. **Structure retrieval:** RCSB PDB gives the protein structures and PubChem gives the drug SMILES strings. It also expands to structurally similar compounds by 3D shape.
  3. **Docking:** DiffDock runs on Runpod serverless GPUs. It scores 10 poses per drug-protein pair and keeps the best confidence.
  4. **Reasoning loop:** Sonar reads each docking round. If it sees patterns, such as one drug class clustering at the top, it decides whether to expand the search or move on to the write-up.
  5. **Report and paper:** It generates a literature review, a results report, and a merged paper with an abstract and citations.
- **Packaging:** A Next.js and shadcn front end has a disease input, a target proteins table, a candidate drugs table, a drug detail view, and a chat-style research assistant. A router agent built on Fetch.ai's uAgents chat protocol lets the pipeline be called from a chat interface.
- **Demo output:** A PDAC (pancreatic cancer) paper docking 70 ligands against KRAS and ERK2. Top hits were KRAS inhibitors such as TH-Z835, BI-3406, divarasib and MRTX1133, plus trametinib for ERK2. It also lists repurposed candidates such as disulfiram, metformin and simvastatin, each with an evidence level.
- **Weakness:** It's validated only by example. The paper says the hits "warrant experimental validation", and many of the top hits are already-known KRAS inhibitors rather than genuine repurposing.

## Half Life (OxHack '26)

- **What it is:** A network-based drug repurposing tool. It won MLH's Best Use of Snowflake API. The live demo is [halflife-bio.vercel.app](https://halflife-bio.vercel.app), and the Devpost is [devpost.com/software/we-ll-figure-out](https://devpost.com/software/we-ll-figure-out).
- **Ranking:** A deterministic algorithm does the ranking, not an LLM. A random walk with restart runs over the STRING protein interaction network, starting from disease proteins from Open Targets. Drug targets come from ChEMBL. The shortlist has 15 candidates (the top 10 by network score plus the top 5 by direct evidence), each with the protein paths that explain it.
- **Jury:** Three LLMs (GPT-5.4, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3) on Snowflake Cortex rank the shortlist from cited evidence, without seeing the network scores.
  - Every reply is validated for valid JSON, real evidence IDs, and exactly quoted numbers.
  - Votes are combined by Borda count, and a consensus needs at least two valid jurors.
- **Docking:** AutoDock Vina docking with a 3Dmol.js viewer is optional, runs on request, and doesn't affect the ranking.
- **Evidence:** Held-out validation and pre-registered tests.
  - The network method finds 15 of 293 approved drugs across 14 diseases, against about 2 for random choice.
  - A blind test with drug names hidden shows only GPT-5.4 and Opus beat chance.
  - The original jury lost to single models, and the README says so.
- **Stack:** FastAPI, React 19, Vite, Tiger Data (Postgres), and Vercel.
- **Team split:** Data and jury, network ranking, and app, backend and docking.

## Ideas for your project summary

1. **Show how the work was checked.** RepoRx shows one demo paper. Half Life hides known approved drugs and checks whether the method ranks them highly. A "rediscovery" benchmark is a strong credibility line for judges.
2. **Say what the LLM does and doesn't do.** Half Life's framing is "ranking comes from data and graph algorithms; AI only reviews". RepoRx lets the LLM drive the loop. Pick one and state it plainly.
3. **Make the output explainable.** Half Life saves the protein paths behind each recommendation. RepoRx cites the literature. Both help a reader trust a result.
4. **Be open about negative results.** Half Life reports that its jury lost and why. That reads as rigorous rather than weak.
5. **Combine them.** The two are complementary: network proximity to shortlist, then docking and literature as supporting evidence, then a cited write-up.
6. **Put the sponsor tech in the summary.** Both projects name the sponsor tools (Runpod, Snowflake Cortex, Perplexity, Fetch.ai) prominently, which matters for sponsor prizes.

What is your HTB26 project? If you tell me the idea or point me at files in this repo, I can draft the summary against these two.

Inspiration
Developing a new medicine can take years of research and testing. Meanwhile, thousands of drugs are already approved for other conditions, with substantial information available about their targets, mechanisms and safety. We wanted to ask a different question: could that existing knowledge help researchers identify which medicines are worth investigating for another disease?

The difficult part isn't producing a list of drugs. It's producing a shortlist that a researcher can interrogate: Why this drug? Which proteins connect it to the disease? What evidence supports the idea, and what evidence argues against it?

We built Half Life at OxHack '26 to bring those answers together.

What it does
A researcher selects a disease. Half Life combines biomedical evidence with a network of human protein interactions to examine existing approved medicines and rank potential Candidates for further study.

The platform:

Connects diseases to biological targets using evidence from Open Targets, then maps approved medicines and their targets using ChEMBL and regulatory drug records.
Ranks Candidates using protein networks. Our application shortlist combines 10 Candidates prioritised by Random Walk with Restart (RWR) on a physical STRING interaction graph with five prioritised by direct disease–target evidence. The original shortest-path and degree-matched z-score rankings remain available for comparison.
Shows the biological connections. For shortlisted Candidates, it reconstructs paths through the protein network, identifying drug targets, intermediate proteins and disease-associated targets. These paths explain network proximity; they are not proof of a therapeutic mechanism or a direct explanation of the RWR calculation.
Challenges the hypothesis with a three-model AI jury. Three distinct models review evidence packets, including mechanisms, pathway context, contradictory findings, safety considerations and missing evidence. Their assessment sits alongside the computational ranking rather than being folded into an invented probability of success.
Explores molecular interactions in 3D. For supported drug–protein pairs, a Docker-based workflow prepares molecular inputs and uses AutoDock Vina with available experimental protein structures to predict binding poses that can be inspected in 3D.
Researchers can compare Candidates, review evidence and preserve reproducible Experiments instead of relying on a single opaque AI answer.

How we built it
We brought together several complementary biomedical resources:

Open Targets for disease–target associations and clinical evidence.
ChEMBL for drugs, molecular identifiers and drug–target relationships.
STRING 12.5 for human protein interaction networks.
Reactome for pathway-level biological context.
RCSB Protein Data Bank for experimentally determined protein structures used in supported docking workflows.
Regulatory sources for approval and safety context.
We constructed our own graph-processing and drug-ranking pipeline. It resolves protein identifiers to stable Ensembl genes, filters and deduplicates STRING interactions, builds reproducible network artifacts and evaluates drug targets against disease-associated targets.

We designed the ranking framework and implemented the algorithms ourselves; we did not invent the underlying mathematics. RWR, shortest-path proximity and degree-matched statistical methods are established techniques. Our engineering contribution is adapting, combining, testing and exposing them in a reproducible disease-specific workflow, including a hybrid 10-plus-5 Candidate-selection policy.

The evidence-review layer uses a three-model jury through Snowflake Cortex. The application connects ranking, evidence review and optional structure-based investigation in a single research workflow.

Challenges we ran into
Biological data does not line up neatly. Different sources use different identifiers, evidence conventions and coverage. Some approved drugs have no usable human targets in our inputs; others fall outside the connected protein network. We had to make missing data explicit instead of quietly giving unsupported drugs misleading scores.

A plausible-looking ranking is not necessarily a good ranking. Our earliest evaluations did not show a clear advantage for degree-matched proximity, so we also tested RWR and a broader functional association network. Expanding the graph improved coverage, but did not automatically prove better retrieval.

Evaluation labels can be wrong or incomplete. We found contradictions between source-reported approval relationships and regulator documentation, and one frozen disease identifier referred to a symptom-measurement trait rather than the intended disease. We preserved the frozen results, documented the issues and kept the conclusions appropriately limited.

Interpretability has limits. A short path between proteins is a real property of our filtered network, but it doesn't demonstrate that a drug treats a disease. Likewise, a docking pose suggests a possible geometric interaction, not clinical efficacy. We designed the interface and jury evidence to maintain those distinctions.

Accomplishments we're proud of
Built and tested a pipeline that processes 1,956 approved Candidates for a disease, with explicit network-coverage reporting.
Implemented both physical-network RWR and alternative rankings, plus reproducible Candidate selection and validated shortest-path explanations.
Developed a versioned evaluation framework with frozen inputs, checksums, baseline comparisons and reproducibility checks.
Ran a 14-case retrospective replication: the physical-RWR shortlist retrieved 15 of 293 recorded reference relationships, compared with 11 of 293 for the original z-score shortlist.
Preserved a scientifically important qualification: the estimated improvement was small and its 95% paired confidence interval included zero. We chose RWR as an application default, not because we proved it was superior.
Validated the integrated ranking workstream with 118 passing automated tests.
What we learned
The biggest lesson was that evidence quality and scientific honesty matter as much as model complexity. A more connected network can cover more drugs without improving every ranking. Three AI models can critique the same hypothesis without constituting independent experimental validation. And a reproducible negative result is more useful than an impressive but unverified claim.

We also learned how much practical work sits between a published biomedical dataset and a usable research tool: identifiers, data lineage, graph coverage, deterministic calculations, test fixtures, model input boundaries and safeguards against overstating conclusions.

What's next
We want to improve reference-label curation, test against genuinely historical datasets where possible, broaden supported drug–protein docking pairs and collect feedback from researchers on which evidence is most useful for deciding what to investigate next.

Our goal is not to replace laboratory experiments or clinical trials. It is to make the earliest stage of drug-repurposing research more focused, transparent and reproducible.

References and resources
The resources below informed our biomedical data pipeline, computational methods, evidence review and structural exploration. The research papers are background and methodological references; we do not claim to have reproduced or implemented their full systems.

Biomedical data and drug information
Open Targets Platform (release 26.09) — disease–Target associations, drug evidence and GraphQL data access: GraphQL API documentation.
ChEMBL (release 37) — approved-drug identifiers, molecular annotations and drug–Target data: ChEMBL database.
STRING (release 12.5) — human physical interaction and functional association network data: STRING downloads.
Reactome — curated biological pathway information: Reactome pathway database.
Ensembl — stable gene identifiers used for cross-database Target mapping: Ensembl.
RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB) — experimentally determined macromolecular structures: RCSB PDB.
PubChem — molecular properties and chemical structure information: PubChem PUG REST API.
FDA Drugs@FDA — US drug approval records: Drugs@FDA.
DailyMed — drug product labels and safety information: DailyMed.
Scientific papers and methodological background
Guney, E., Menche, J., Vidal, M. & Barabási, A.-L. (2016). Network-based in silico drug efficacy screening. Nature Communications, 7, 10331. Paper / DOI.
Wang, Z. et al. (2025). DeepEvidence: Empowering Biomedical Discovery with Deep Knowledge Graph Research. arXiv:2601.11560. Paper (PDF).

The Cure That Was Already There
A potential cancer treatment sat in medicine cabinets for 50 years before anyone noticed. Metformin, one of the most common diabetes drugs in the world, wasn't investigated for pancreatic cancer until 2005 — half a century after FDA approval. We’re making sure that never happens again.

We’re focusing on repurposing already FDA-approved drugs. Developing a new cancer drug through the FDA approval process typically takes 10–15 years and over $1 billion, creating a major bottleneck for patients who urgently need better treatments. Repurposing already FDA-approved drugs offers an easier path.

Recently, there are new tools to simulate drugs and their effectiveness in targeting cancer, but the research space is simply too large to try all of them.

So we built, RepoRx, a research platform for discovering potential cancer treatments in drugs that were never designed for cancer.

See more about the why here.

What it does
Our agents

Compose a full literature review that synthesizes current research
Identify proteins to target, and relevant drugs
Run experiments to simulate the interaction between the proteins and compounds
Output:

Full research report to share
Simulation results that show the most promising drugs to take to wet labs
Confidence scores assigned to each drug candidate
Once the outputs are received, researchers can take them to the wet lab or continue searching for compounds with similar molecular structures in order to find more potential drugs – right on our platform.

How we built it
We built a modular, multi-agent pipeline in TypeScript with a Next.js + Tailwind frontend. The app is hosted on Vercel. Each agent handles a distinct phase of the workflow and communicates via structured JSON, allowing independent development, debugging, and resumable execution.
Orchestrated agent flows using Fetch.ai – registered an agent on AgentVerse where it can be used in ASI:One, an alternative UI to our platform.
Using the arXiv API and Perplexity AI (Sonar Pro Deep Research), the system synthesizes current research for a selected cancer type and extracts high-impact protein targets (e.g., EGFR, KRAS, p53), along with known drugs, mechanisms of action, and FDA status.
The agent retrieves high-resolution protein structures from the RCSB Protein Data Bank and queries PubChem to collect and expand candidate compounds. RDKit canonicalizes SMILES - strings for docking compatibility.
We run DiffDock on RunPod serverless GPUs (Nvidia Blackwells) to predict protein–ligand binding. Ligands are processed in parallel batches, generating multiple poses per pair and ranking candidates by confidence score (0–1).
Docking results are classified into cancer-approved drugs, repurposing candidates, and novel compounds. The system generates a ranked repurposing leaderboard and automatically produces structured research summaries using Perplexity AI. A final assistant agent explains the results and future recommendations interactively.
Challenges we ran into
Running DiffDock locally wasn’t feasible due to GPU and memory limitations. We had to provision cloud infrastructure on RunPod and deploy to virtual NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs to handle large-scale docking simulations. This required setting up remote job orchestration, batching, and polling logic under tight time constraints.
DiffDock requires clean, consistent structural inputs. Converting compounds from PubChem into canonicalized SMILES and compatible 3D formats introduced edge cases (naming conflicts, malformed structures, conversion mismatches). Ensuring filesystem-safe ligand naming while preserving metadata required additional preprocessing and validation layers.
We initially built the backend in Python (Flask), but migrated to a full TypeScript stack mid-hackathon for better compatibility with Vercel deployment and frontend integration. This required refactoring API orchestration, async workflows, and agent communication under time pressure.
Because our system surfaces drug recommendations in a clinical domain, we had to think carefully about disclaimers, scope limitation, and responsible framing. Determining where human oversight is required—and ensuring the system is positioned as a research aid rather than a clinical decision-maker—was an important design consideration.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We built a system that takes a single cancer-type input and autonomously performs literature synthesis, target identification, structure retrieval, compound discovery, molecular docking with DiffDock, classification, and report generation—compressing what typically a lab takes weeks or months to research into one automated workflow that completes in several minutes.
We deployed real large-scale docking simulations on cloud GPUs via RunPod, using a physics-informed diffusion model, generating ranked confidence scores across multiple protein–drug pairs in parallel.
Despite migrating tech stacks mid-hackathon and provisioning GPU infrastructure from scratch, we delivered a production-style TypeScript backend with a deployable Next.js frontend.
What we learned
Building in the medical domain forced us to think beyond technical performance. Even though our system is research-focused, surfacing drug recommendations carries real-world implications. We learned the importance of positioning the platform as a decision-support tool and not an authority, clearly defining its scope.
In healthcare, outputs can influence high-stakes decisions. We had to consider disclaimers, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and how recommendations are communicated.
What's next
We plan to incorporate patient-specific safety constraints, including pre-existing conditions, contraindications, and known adverse interaction profiles. This will allow the system to filter or down-rank compounds that may pose elevated clinical risk, improving real-world viability.
We want to make the workflow fully iterative: allowing users to move forward or backward between stages (e.g., refining target selection after docking results, expanding compound libraries, or re-running simulations with adjusted constraints).
For top-ranked candidates, we aim to integrate more rigorous physics-based methods beyond DiffDock, such as molecular dynamics simulations and free-energy calculations, to improve binding accuracy and reduce false positives.
Once computational confidence is strengthened, the next step is structured recommendation for wet-lab validation prioritizing compounds with strong predicted binding, established safety profiles, and mechanistic plausibility for in vitro testing.

- **Limits stated plainly:** A short path in the network is not proof a drug treats the disease, and a docking pose is not clinical efficacy. The jury sits beside the ranking and isn't folded into an invented probability of success.
- **Data problems:** They hit identifier mismatches, drugs with no usable human targets, contradictory approval labels, and one frozen disease ID that turned out to be a symptom-measurement trait.

What do these do in general? What is the problem they are trying to solve? How are they solving the same?

Both projects work on **drug repurposing**: finding new uses for medicines that are already approved.

## The problem they're solving

- Developing a new drug takes about 10–15 years and over $1B.
- Thousands of approved drugs already have known safety profiles and known protein targets.
- Some of those drugs may work on other diseases, but nobody knows which ones. Metformin sat for about 50 years before anyone tested it on pancreatic cancer.
- The search space is far too big to test by hand or in the lab. Researchers need a short, prioritised list of drugs worth testing next.

Neither project claims to prove a drug works. Both aim to narrow thousands of drugs down to a handful worth a researcher's time.

## How each one solves it

| | **RepoRx** (TreeHacks 2026) | **Half Life** (OxHack '26) |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Cancer, one type at a time | Any disease |
| **Core idea** | Simulate whether each drug physically fits the disease's target protein | Measure how close a drug's targets sit to the disease's proteins in the human protein-interaction network |
| **Step 1** | AI reads the literature to find the disease's key target proteins, such as KRAS | Open Targets lists the disease's proteins and ChEMBL lists each drug's proteins |
| **Step 2** | Fetch each protein's 3D structure and the drugs' chemical structures | Place both on the STRING protein-interaction network |
| **Step 3** | DiffDock, an AI docking model on cloud GPUs, predicts how each drug binds and gives a confidence score | A random walk with restart scores each drug, and a drug scores high if its targets are close to the disease's proteins |
| **Step 4** | An AI loop spots patterns, such as a drug class clustering at the top, and decides whether to expand the search | Three AI models, blind to the scores, review the shortlist's evidence and vote |
| **Output** | A ranked leaderboard and a full AI-written research paper | 15 candidates, each with the protein paths that explain it, plus an optional 3D docking view |
| **Character** | Automated and end-to-end | Careful and explainable |

In short, RepoRx asks whether a drug can physically bind the disease's target, while Half Life asks whether the drug's targets are biologically close to the disease.

## What they have in common

- **Staging:** Both go from a disease to biological targets, then to candidate drugs, then to evidence, then to a shortlist.
- **Docking:** Both use molecular docking, though RepoRx relies on it and Half Life treats it as optional.
- **Human review:** Both end by handing the shortlist to a researcher and make no clinical claims.
- **Honesty:** Both state their limits. A docking pose or a short network path is not proof a drug treats the disease.

The main difference is trust. RepoRx's output is a docking confidence score and an AI-written paper. Half Life checks whether its method can rediscover drugs already approved for a disease, and it reports that the improvement over the baseline was small and not statistically certain.

So based on this, what could be further improvements that could be made to such simulations

These ideas come from the gaps both projects admit to, plus general limits of these methods.

## 1. Better ranking and evidence

- **Combine the signals.** RepoRx's docking and Half Life's network proximity measure different things (physical binding vs biological closeness), and neither project merges them. A drug that scores well on both is a stronger candidate. Fusing them with a learned or weighted model is the clearest gap.
- **Use direction of effect.** Both mostly ask whether a drug is *near* the disease. They don't ask whether it *activates or inhibits* the target, or whether the disease needs that target turned up or down. An inhibitor of an overactive protein is a real lead, while an activator of the same protein could make things worse.
- **Add other data types.** Gene expression shifts (such as LINCS or Connectivity Map signatures), real-world patient data, and trial records could back up or contradict the network and docking scores.
- **Try graph neural networks and knowledge-graph embeddings.** Half Life cites KG-bench, which benchmarks these methods. They could replace or sit beside random walk with restart.
- **Handle drugs with no known targets.** Half Life can't score 557 of 1,956 drugs on the network. Predicting likely targets from chemical structure would close that gap.

## 2. Better docking and simulation

- **Dock against more than one structure.** Proteins are flexible. Docking to a single PDB structure can miss or invent binding modes. Ensemble docking, or AlphaFold/Boltz-style predicted structures for proteins with no experimental one, would help.
- **Re-score the top hits.** Docking confidence is a weak predictor on its own. Both projects name physics-based refinement as a next step: molecular dynamics, free-energy perturbation (FEP/MM-GBSA), and consensus scoring across several docking tools.
- **Check selectivity.** A drug that binds the disease target but also binds many other proteins may cause side effects. Docking against anti-targets (hERG, CYP enzymes) and off-targets would flag those.
- **Account for the tumour mutation.** Variants like KRAS G12D change the binding pocket. Dock against the mutant form, not a generic structure.

## 3. Safety and real-world viability

- **Filter by safety and exposure.** Check that the drug reaches the tissue at the dose needed. Include known contraindications, adverse event reports (FAERS), drug–drug interactions, and patient-specific constraints, which RepoRx lists as future work.
- **Include ADMET prediction.** Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity models can down-rank candidates before any lab work.
- **Look at combinations.** Many repurposed drugs work in pairs or as a boost to standard chemotherapy, and single-drug ranking misses that.

## 4. Validation, the biggest weakness

- **Use genuinely historical tests.** Rank using only data from before a given year, then check whether drugs later shown to work rise to the top. Half Life names this as a next step. It avoids data leakage.
- **Evaluate harder and report uncertainty.** Add more diseases, wider confidence intervals, and ablations showing which signal helps. Half Life already models this. RepoRx has none: it shows one example paper and no benchmark.
- **Clean the labels.** Half Life found contradictory approval records and a wrong disease ID. Better curated ground truth would make every metric more meaningful.
- **Link to wet-lab results.** Cell-line sensitivity databases (GDSC, DepMap) give cheap computational validation, and a small partnership for real assays would give actual validation.

## 5. Handling LLM limits

- **Check citations.** Half Life validates every jury quote. RepoRx's AI-written paper cites sources but has no verification step, and generated papers can fabricate or misattribute claims.
- **Keep model refusals from skewing results.** Half Life's jury lost partly because a safety filter refused about half of one model's calls. Plan for that up front.
- **Use LLMs for explanation, not scoring.** Half Life's blind test showed models do well partly because they recognise drug names. Hiding names, or keeping the models out of the ranking, avoids that.

## 6. Workflow and usability

- **Let researchers iterate.** Allow going back a stage, such as refining targets after seeing docking results or expanding the compound library.
- **Make runs reproducible.** Versioned data, checksums and saved experiments (Half Life does this) should be standard for any platform like this.
- **Collect feedback.** Ask researchers what evidence they'd actually use to decide what to test next, and tune the output to that.

## If you can only do a few

1. **Fuse network and docking signals,** since each project has only one half.
2. **Run a historical or retrospective benchmark with confidence intervals.**
3. **Add a safety and off-target filter** so the shortlist is realistic to test.

Is it possible to create a project that deals with antibiotics and antibiotics resistance, and coming up with possible solutions, and whether there are signals that we could use to try to generate new drugs

Yes, this is feasible and a good fit. It has the same shape as the two projects you looked at, and it has better public data in some areas.

## The problem

- Bacteria are evolving resistance faster than new antibiotics are approved. The pipeline of truly new classes is thin, and few companies invest in it because the return is poor.
- Resistance is driven by a small set of recognisable mechanisms: enzymes that destroy the drug (beta-lactamases), efflux pumps, altered targets (mutated PBPs, gyrase, ribosome), and reduced uptake.
- The WHO priority pathogens, especially the ESKAPE group (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter), are where the need is greatest.

## What a project could do

Three angles, ordered from most achievable to most ambitious. You could take one or chain them.

1. **Resistance-aware repurposing and combinations.** This is the closest match to Half Life and RepoRx. Given a resistant strain's genome, identify which resistance mechanisms it carries, then recommend approved drugs, or drug combinations, that evade them. Examples include a beta-lactam plus a beta-lactamase inhibitor, or an efflux-pump inhibitor paired with an antibiotic.
2. **Resistance surveillance and forecasting.** Track which resistance genes and mutations are rising by species, region and year. Flag emerging threats and drugs that are losing effectiveness.
3. **New-drug generation.** Use the signals below to propose new molecules, or antimicrobial peptides, predicted to kill resistant bacteria. Rank them by predicted activity, toxicity to human cells, and whether known resistance mechanisms would defeat them.

## Signals that could guide new-drug generation

| Signal | What it tells you | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| **Essential genes** | Targets the bacterium can't live without, and so are harder to bypass | Essential-gene databases such as DEG and transposon-sequencing studies |
| **Target conservation** | Whether a target is shared across many pathogens (broad spectrum) or absent in humans (lower toxicity) | Comparative genomics, BV-BRC |
| **Resistance gene and mutation profile** | Which drug classes already fail against a strain, and which mechanisms a new molecule must avoid | CARD, ResFinder, AMRFinderPlus |
| **MIC and growth-inhibition data** | Ground truth for which molecules actually kill which strains | Public susceptibility datasets, CO-ADD, ChEMBL bioactivity |
| **Collateral sensitivity** | Resistance to drug A makes the bacterium *more* sensitive to drug B | Published evolution experiments |
| **Synergy data** | Pairs that work together and suppress resistance | Combination screens in the literature |
| **Structure and chemistry** | Which molecular substructures drive killing, so new drugs can be designed around them | Explainable models trained on activity data |
| **Antimicrobial peptide sequences** | Natural templates for peptide design | DBAASP, APD3 |

Published work shows this approach can succeed. Machine-learning screens led by the Collins and Stokes groups found halicin and abaucin, and later work used explainable models to identify a new structural class of antibiotic. That gives you credible precedent in your summary.

## A possible pipeline

1. **Input:** a pathogen, or an uploaded resistant isolate's genome or gene list.
2. **Resistance profiling:** detect resistance genes and mutations with AMRFinderPlus or CARD, then map them to the drugs they defeat.
3. **Target selection:** pick essential, conserved, non-human targets, and check structures in the PDB.
4. **Candidate generation:** either screen existing compounds from ChEMBL and DrugBank, or generate new molecules with a generative model.
5. **Scoring:**
   - predicted activity from a model trained on public bioactivity data;
   - docking against the target, and against the mutated version if the isolate has a target mutation;
   - toxicity and ADMET filters;
   - a "resistance risk" score: would a known mechanism defeat it?
6. **Explanation:** show the resistance mechanisms present, why each candidate evades them, and the evidence behind it.
7. **Output:** a ranked shortlist for lab testing.

## How it could stand out

- **Resistance risk as a first-class signal.** Neither Half Life nor RepoRx considers whether the target will mutate away. For antibiotics that is the central issue.
- **A retrospective test.** Hide a drug class that was approved after a given year and check whether the method would have ranked it highly, as Half Life did with approved drugs.
- **Honest limits.** Say that predicted activity in a computer isn't a working antibiotic. Real bacteria have outer membranes and efflux pumps that stop many molecules reaching their targets, and this is one of the main reasons computational hits fail in the lab.

## Risks and cautions

- **Gram-negative bacteria are hard.** Docking success often fails because the molecule can't get in. A model of cell entry, or training on whole-cell data, matters more than target docking alone.
- **Data quality and bias.** Surveillance data is uneven across regions, and labels can be noisy or inconsistent.
- **Scope.** Don't try all three angles for a hackathon. One angle done well, with a validation test, beats three half-built.
- **Responsible use.** Keep the tool aimed at finding and defeating resistance, such as profiling isolates and ranking treatments. Don't build features that help design or enhance resistant or more dangerous organisms.

## A realistic hackathon scope

Build angle 1 for a small set of pathogens, say three ESKAPE species. Use CARD to profile resistance genes, map them to drug classes, and rank approved drugs and combinations with a simple explanation. Add one validation test and a clear statement of what the output does and doesn't mean. If time allows, add a docking step against one well-characterised target like a penicillin-binding protein.

# Scope: Antibiotic Resistance, In-Silico Candidate Discovery

Working scope for Hack The Burgh 2026. It builds on the idea in [README.md](README.md) and picks a disease target (antibiotic-resistant bacteria) plus the sponsor tracks worth aiming at.

## 1. Problem

- Bacteria are evolving resistance faster than new antibiotic classes are approved, and the pipeline of new classes is thin.
- Resistance comes from a small set of recognisable mechanisms: drug-destroying enzymes (beta-lactamases), efflux pumps, altered targets (mutated PBPs, gyrase, ribosome) and reduced uptake.
- Highest need: the WHO priority pathogens, especially the ESKAPE group.
- Wet-lab screening is slow and expensive, so researchers need a short, explained, prioritised list of candidates worth testing.

## 2. One-line pitch

Given a resistant bacterium, profile *why* it is resistant, then rank approved drugs, combinations and (stretch) new molecules that are predicted to evade those mechanisms, and show the evidence behind each pick, all in silico.

## 3. Reference projects

| | RepoRx (TreeHacks 26) | Half Life (OxHack 26) | Us |
|---|---|---|---|
| Method | DiffDock docking + LLM literature agents | Network proximity (RWR on STRING) + LLM jury | Resistance profiling + target/docking + predicted activity |
| Strength | End-to-end automation | Honest validation | (aim for both) |
| Gap | No benchmark | One signal, no docking-led ranking | Add resistance risk as a first-class signal |

## 4. Candidate signals (what we can score on)

| Signal | Source |
|---|---|
| Resistance genes and mutations present | CARD, ResFinder, AMRFinderPlus |
| Essential, conserved, non-human targets | DEG, comparative genomics (BV-BRC) |
| Known activity (MIC, growth inhibition) | ChEMBL, CO-ADD, public susceptibility data |
| Collateral sensitivity and synergy | Published evolution and combination screens |
| Target structure, wild type and mutant | RCSB PDB |
| Toxicity and ADMET filters | Public models and rules |
| Antimicrobial peptide templates | DBAASP, APD3 |

## 5. MVP (must ship)

1. Input: a species (3 ESKAPE pathogens) or a list of resistance genes.
2. Resistance profile: map genes to the drug classes they defeat.
3. Ranked shortlist of approved drugs and drug combinations that avoid those mechanisms, each with an explanation (mechanism evaded, evidence, caveats).
4. One retrospective validation test, with the confidence or uncertainty reported honestly.
5. Clear limits statement: a computational hit is not a working antibiotic.

## 6. Stretch (only if MVP is done)

- Docking against one well-characterised target (for example a PBP) using AutoDock Vina, including a mutant structure.
- Resistance-risk score: would a known mechanism defeat this candidate?
- Generative step: propose new molecules or peptides, filtered by predicted activity and toxicity.
- Interactive 3D view of the protein-drug pose.

## 7. Out of scope

- Any claim of clinical efficacy or dosing advice.
- Features that help design or enhance resistant or more dangerous organisms.
- Gram-negative cell-entry modelling beyond a simple filter.
- Wet-lab validation.

## 8. Validation plan

Matches the third point in the README ("test on past diseases"):

- Hide a drug (or class) approved after a cutoff year, or a known effective combination for a pathogen.
- Check whether the method ranks it near the top, compared with a random baseline and a simple baseline (for example ranking by known resistance only).
- Report the rate found and a confidence interval. A small or uncertain result is acceptable if stated plainly.

## 9. Track fit

Prizes and challenge names are read from the sponsor slide. Details of the judging criteria still need confirming with the sponsors.

| Sponsor | Challenge | Fit | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HRT** | Best Use of Data for Predictions & Decision Making | **Strong. Primary.** | The project is a ranking and decision tool built on data. The retrospective test, confidence intervals and a resistance-forecasting view all speak to "predictions and decision making". |
| **G-Research** | Make the invisible visible | **Good. Secondary.** | Resistance mechanisms, protein networks and binding poses are invisible to non-experts. A clear visual layer (resistance map, network paths, 3D pose) fits the brief. Needs real design effort. |
| **Wordsmith** | Most complicated end-to-end agentic AI browser-use workflow | **Possible, risky.** | An agent could browse CARD, NCBI and PDB to gather evidence. It would only count if the browser-use is central and complex. Don't add it just for the prize. Decide early. |
| **JetBrains** | Help the Developer | Poor | Not a developer tool. |
| **Instalily** | Coding agent that adapts to its user | Poor | Different problem. |
| **Bank of Scotland** | Smart Cost of Living | Poor | No natural link. |
| **Viridien** | Lithological interval detection, depth mapping, legend classification | Poor | Geology and well-log data, unrelated. |

### Recommendation

- **Aim for HRT first, G-Research second.** One build serves both: a ranking engine plus a visual explanation layer.
- Treat Wordsmith as an optional add-on, only if an agentic data-gathering step is needed anyway.
- Ignore the other four.

## 10. Open decisions

- [ ] Final disease or pathogen set (suggest three ESKAPE species).
- [ ] Which signals make the MVP (suggest resistance profile + one activity or target signal).
- [ ] Which retrospective test to run (needs a data check first).
- [ ] Decision on Wordsmith: in or out.
- [ ] Team roles: data and validation, ranking engine, front end and visuals.
- [ ] Hackathon time budget, to size the stretch goals.

## 11. Main risks

- Docking has weak predictive power on its own, so avoid leaning on it as the headline.
- Public data is uneven and some labels are noisy, so plan for cleaning time.
- A pretty interface over a weak result will not score well on HRT. Validation comes first.
- Scope creep into generation. Do not start it before the MVP works.

| **Wordsmith**: complicated agentic browser-use workflow | **Possible but risky** | An agent could gather evidence from CARD, NCBI and PDB, but it only counts if the browser use is central and complex. |
| **JetBrains**, **Instalily**, **Bank of Scotland**, **Viridien** | **Poor** | None has a natural link: developer tooling, a coding agent, cost of living, and geological well-log analysis. |

My recommendation is to target HRT first and G-Research second. One build can serve both: a ranking engine plus a visual explanation layer. Treat Wordsmith as an optional add-on.

## What's in the scope file

- **Problem and pitch:** a one-line version of the antibiotic-resistance idea.
- **Comparison:** the project against RepoRx and Half Life.
- **Signals:** the data we could score on, with sources.
- **MVP, stretch and out-of-scope lists:** the MVP is a resistance profile, a ranked shortlist with explanations, and one validation test. The stretch is docking and a generative step.
- **Validation plan:** hide a known drug or drug class and check whether the method ranks it near the top.
- **Open decisions and risks:** a checklist of choices still to make.

## Caveats

- I read the prizes and challenge names off the slide photo. The judging criteria are not on it, so confirm those with the sponsors before committing, especially for HRT and G-Research.
- Which retrospective test is feasible depends on the data available, and I haven't checked that yet.

Decision for you: whether to include Wordsmith. I'd say no unless you'd build an agentic data-gathering step anyway. Say if you want me to add anything to the scope or tighten the MVP.

content.text:
Written for: you and your team, to decide what to reuse and what to build.

Before you reuse any code, check three things:
- **tree26 is MIT-licensed.** You can reuse it with attribution.
- **Half Life has no licence file.** Without one, the default is all rights reserved. Ask the authors, or reimplement the ideas yourself.
- **Check the HTB26 rules** on pre-existing code. Many hackathons require that the work is new, or that reused code is declared. Reusing methods is the safer route either way.

## Can be adopted

| Piece | From | What to take | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Structure retrieval** | tree26 (`agent2.py`) | RCSB PDB search and download, PubChem SMILES lookup, RDKit canonicalisation | Plain REST calls with no LLM. Usable almost as is (MIT). Swap the inputs from cancer proteins to bacterial targets. |
| **Docking runner** | tree26 (`agent3.py`) | Batching, parallel jobs, polling, confidence normalisation | Only if you use DiffDock on Runpod. Half Life used AutoDock Vina in Docker instead, which is cheaper and local. |
| **Pipeline orchestration** | tree26 (`pipeline.py`) | Staged agents passing structured JSON, resumable state | A pattern worth keeping, whichever language you write it in. |
| **Evidence-review layer** | Half Life idea | An LLM or jury reading cited evidence, with validation of every reply (valid JSON, real evidence IDs, exact numbers) | Reimplement the pattern. The citation checks are the valuable part. |
| **Validation method** | Half Life idea | Frozen inputs, a hidden-known-answer test, baselines, confidence intervals | Mostly a method to copy, not code. Their `results/` protocols are a good template. |
| **Ranking baselines** | Half Life idea | Random-walk-with-restart and z-score on a protein network | Only useful if you also use a network signal. Not essential for the MVP. |
| **3D viewer** | Half Life idea | 3Dmol.js for displaying poses | A small, easy front-end piece. |
| **App scaffolding** | Both | Half Life's FastAPI + React structure and fixture-based offline mode, or tree26's Next.js + shadcn front end | Pick one stack and stay with it. tree26 migrated mid-hackathon and found it costly. |
| **Responsible framing** | Both | "Research aid, not clinical decision-maker" disclaimers and a clear limits statement | Copy the approach, not the wording. |

## To build from scratch

| Piece | Why it's new |
|---|---|
| **Resistance profiling** | Neither project touches resistance. You need to ingest CARD, ResFinder or AMRFinderPlus and map each gene or mutation to the drug classes it defeats. This is the core of the project. |
| **Pathogen and target selection** | Both reference projects work from human disease proteins. You need bacterial targets that are essential, conserved and absent in humans, with their PDB structures. |
| **Antibiotic drug data** | You need antibiotic classes, mechanisms of action, MIC and susceptibility data, and combination or synergy records. ChEMBL has some, but the resistance link has to be built. |
| **Resistance-aware ranking** | The scoring logic that says whether a candidate evades the mechanisms present. It's your main contribution, so there's nothing to borrow. |
| **Resistance-risk score** | Whether a target is likely to mutate away. The reference projects have no equivalent. |
| **Retrospective test design** | The idea is borrowed, but the test itself is new: which antibiotic or combination to hide, with what cutoff, from which data. This needs a data check first. |
| **Mutant-aware docking (stretch)** | Docking against the mutated structure when an isolate has a target mutation. |
| **Generative step (stretch)** | Neither project generates new molecules. Both rank existing ones. |
| **Safety and toxicity filters** | Human-cell toxicity and ADMET screens. RepoRx lists them as future work. |
| **Visual layer for G-Research** | Resistance map, mechanism diagrams and an explanation view. The reference UIs are drug tables and a chat, not what the track asks for. |

## What this means in practice

- **Around 30–40% can be borrowed,** mostly plumbing: structure fetching, docking, orchestration, the viewer and the app skeleton.
- **The part that earns the prize is new.** Resistance data, the ranking logic and the validation are all yours.
- **Starting point:** if the team is Python-comfortable, begin with tree26's `agent2.py` and Half Life's validation approach. That gets you structures and a test harness in the first few hours.

The scope file has a related MVP list. Should I add a "reuse vs build" section to [scope.md](scope.md), or sketch the repo layout and first-day task split from this?
Go ahead. There is permission from half life and you can use it without credit

## 10. Reuse vs build

Licensing and permission:

- **Half Life:** the authors have given permission to reuse it, with no credit required.
- **tree26 (RepoRx):** MIT-licensed. Reuse is fine, but keep its licence notice in any file or substantial copy taken from it.
- Still check the HTB26 rules on pre-existing code and declare reuse if required.

### Adopt

| Piece | From | What to take |
|---|---|---|
| Structure retrieval | tree26 `agent2.py` | RCSB PDB search and download, PubChem SMILES lookup, RDKit canonicalisation. Swap in bacterial targets. |
| Docking runner (optional) | tree26 `agent3.py` | Batching, parallel jobs, polling, confidence normalisation, if using DiffDock on Runpod. |
| Pipeline orchestration | tree26 `pipeline.py` | Staged steps passing structured JSON, resumable state. |
| API and app skeleton | Half Life `app/api`, `app/web` | FastAPI + React layout, fixture-based offline mode, job handling. |
| Docking and 3D view | Half Life docking workflow, 3Dmol.js | AutoDock Vina in Docker, pose viewer. |
| Evidence jury and validators | Half Life `core/jury` | Prompting and validation of replies (valid JSON, real evidence IDs, exact numbers, Borda vote). |
| Validation harness | Half Life `results/`, evaluation scripts | Frozen inputs, baselines, confidence intervals, reproducibility checks. |
| Network ranking (optional) | Half Life ranking code | RWR and z-score, only if a protein-network signal is added. |
| Tests and reproducibility habits | Half Life | Test layout, checksums, fixtures. |

### Build from scratch

| Piece | Why |
|---|---|
| Resistance profiling | Neither project handles resistance. Ingest CARD, ResFinder or AMRFinderPlus and map each gene or mutation to the drug classes it defeats. This is the core. |
| Pathogen and target selection | Reference projects use human disease proteins. Need essential, conserved, non-human bacterial targets with PDB structures. |
| Antibiotic data layer | Antibiotic classes, mechanisms, MIC and susceptibility data, synergy records, linked to resistance mechanisms. |
| Resistance-aware ranking | Scoring that decides whether a candidate evades the mechanisms present. |
| Resistance-risk score | Likelihood a target mutates away. |
| Retrospective test design | Which drug or combination to hide, with what cutoff, from which data. |
| Mutant-aware docking (stretch) | Dock against the mutated structure. |
| Generative step (stretch) | Neither reference project generates molecules. |
| Safety and toxicity filters | Human-cell toxicity and ADMET screens. |
| Resistance visual layer | Resistance map, mechanism view and explanations for the G-Research track. |

Rough split: plumbing is borrowed, while the data, ranking and validation that make the project distinct are new.

### Suggested layout

```
/data          raw downloads (CARD, ChEMBL, PDB) and cached derived files, not committed if large
/core
  resistance/  profiling: genes and mutations -> drug classes defeated
  targets/     essential and conserved target selection, structure retrieval
  ranking/     resistance-aware scoring and baselines
  evidence/    LLM review and citation validators
  docking/     Vina or DiffDock runner (stretch)
/eval          retrospective test, frozen inputs, baselines, results
/app
  api/         FastAPI endpoints
  web/         React front end, resistance map and 3D viewer
/docs          method notes and limits statement
```

## 11. Open decisions

Mostly yes. The ignore rules came across from Half Life correctly, but tree26's generated files weren't covered, so I added them.

**What was already fine**
- `.env` is ignored and `.env.example` is kept. No real `.env` is in the copied files.
- Python junk (`.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `.pytest_cache/`, `*.pyc`, `*.egg-info/`) is ignored.

- `app/web/.gitignore` came across with the front end and ignores `node_modules/` and `dist/`.

**What I fixed**
- tree26's `pipeline.py` writes its outputs into whichever directory it runs from. Those files were not ignored. I added rules for `pipeline_state.json`, `structures/`, `agent*_output.json`, `review.md`, `review.json`, `results.md` and `final_paper.md` inside `core/discovery_pipeline/`.
- I checked that the new rules match those outputs and don't match `results.py`, which is real source.

**Things to know**
- The `.gitignore` rules only cover `core/discovery_pipeline/`. If you run the pipeline from the repo root, the outputs land there and show up as untracked.
- About 490 files are untracked. The biggest are the frozen result JSONs in `results/`, around 4 MB each, plus `uv.lock` and some PDB files. That's fine for git, but it makes the first commit large.
- The `.gitattributes` I copied keeps `results/**` out of line-ending conversion, because Half Life's hashes depend on exact bytes. Leave it as is.

Yes. I appended a "Pipeline" section with a Mermaid flowchart to [README.md](README.md) and left your existing notes untouched.

I haven't rendered it. It uses basic flowchart syntax, so GitHub and VS Code's Markdown preview should show it. Check it in the preview and tell me if anything looks off.

**Main path:**
1. Input is a pathogen or a list of resistance genes.
2. Resistance profiling maps genes to the drug classes they defeat.
3. Target selection picks essential, conserved bacterial targets.
4. Structure retrieval fetches structures from PDB and PubChem.
5. A candidate pool of approved drugs and combinations feeds into resistance-aware ranking.
6. Evidence review checks the ranking against cited evidence.
7. The output is a ranked shortlist with explanations, shown with a resistance map, evidence and a 3D pose.

**Colour coding:**
- **Blue:** new work (resistance profiling, target selection, candidate pool, ranking, validation).
- **Grey:** reused code (structure retrieval, evidence review, shortlist output).
- **Dashed:** stretch goals (docking against wild-type and mutant targets, generating new molecules).

The retrospective validation test is drawn as a side input to the ranking step.

The grey labels are rough. "Shortlist" reuses Half Life's output format, but the ranking logic feeding it is new. The legend text above the diagram says the same.

# oxhack-worker: the AutoDock Vina docking worker

Computes binding poses for the app (plan.md section 7, docs/engineering/build-reference.md
C1-C9). A pose is a geometric hypothesis and a Vina score is a rough, unitless
estimate of fit: neither is a measured binding affinity, probability of binding
or clinical effect.

## How it fits together

Two Pythons are involved, because Vina publishes Linux x86_64 wheels only:

| Module | Runs in | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `oxhack_worker.prepare` | docking venv | Downloads each structure from RCSB and writes `structures/{PDB}/` (committed) and `structures/settings.json`. |
| `oxhack_worker.dock` | docking venv | Docks one SMILES into one structure; writes `poses.sdf`, `scores.json`, `log.txt` and copies of `receptor.pdb` and `crystal_ligand.sdf`. |
| `oxhack_worker.control` | docking venv | The symmetry-aware RMSD (RDKit) to the crystal pose, and a command that redocks a structure's crystal ligand by hand. |
| `oxhack_worker.queue` | project venv (`uv run`) | The docking worker: claims `dock_jobs`, runs `dock` as a subprocess, stores the files and the result. |

With `OXHACK_DOCKING=vina` (which needs `OXHACK_REPO=postgres`):

1. The API lists the structures in `structures/` and queues a docking request as a
   `dock_jobs` row. Its `cache_key` is the SHA-256 of the PDB ID, chain, SMILES,
   box, engine, engine version, exhaustiveness and seed; an identical request gets
   a new row that reuses the first job's result (`cached_from`). An Experiment may
   have at most 3 computations queued or running.
2. Every process seeds one queued `redock_control` job per structure, with an ID
   derived from its cache key, so the control is measured once per toolchain.
3. The docking worker claims the oldest queued row with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
   It runs `python -m oxhack_worker.dock` with `$DOCKING_VENV/bin/python` in its
   own process group and kills the group after `OXHACK_DOCK_TIMEOUT_S` (180 s).
4. On success the files move to `$RESULTS_DIR/{job_id}/`; the row gets the
   scores, each file's SHA-256 and, for a control, the top pose's RMSD. The API
   serves the files from `/api/files/{job_id}/{name}` and shows the control's
   measured RMSD as passed (at most 2.0 angstroms) or failed. On a timeout or an
   error the row is `failed` with the last lines of stderr.
5. A job whose worker dies is re-queued after `OXHACK_JOB_STALE_AFTER_S`, and
   failed after `OXHACK_JOB_MAX_ATTEMPTS` claims. The pipeline worker
   (`python -m oxhack_api.worker`) does not touch `dock_jobs` in this mode.

The default, `OXHACK_DOCKING=fixture`, keeps the made-up fixture results and never

## What needs installing

**Core, to run the copied Half Life app on its sample data (no accounts or keys needed):**

| Tool | Version | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11 or newer | API, ranking, jury |
| [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | already on your machine (0.11.19) | Manages the Python workspace. Run `uv sync --all-packages` once. |
| Node.js | 22.22 or newer | The React front end (`cd app/web && npm install && npm run dev`) |

Running `uv sync` pulls in FastAPI, uvicorn, pydantic, DuckDB, NumPy, SciPy, `openai` and the rest. `npm install` pulls in the web dependencies. Playwright browsers (`npx playwright install`) are only needed for the end-to-end tests.

**Optional, depending on what you switch on:**

| Tool | Needed for |
|---|---|
| Docker | The AutoDock Vina docking worker. Vina publishes Linux x86_64 wheels only, so it can't run natively on your Apple Silicon Mac. |
| PostgreSQL (Tiger Data or similar) | Persistent storage and the docking job queue. Memory storage is the default. |
| Snowflake Cortex account and token | The live model jury. A fixture or mock jury works without it. |
| RDKit | Already pinned in the worker. The tree26 scripts also need it. |
| Vercel CLI | Deployment only |

**For the tree26 scripts in `core/discovery_pipeline/`:** these are not part of the uv workspace. They have their own `requirements.txt`: `requests`, `python-dotenv`, `runpod`, `rdkit`, `gemmi`, `pytest`, and `uagents` plus `uagents-core`. The last two are for the Fetch.ai chat agent, so skip them unless you want that. Their API keys (Perplexity, Runpod) are only needed if you run the literature and DiffDock steps, and you may not.

Both servers are background processes. Stop them with `pkill -f uvicorn` and `pkill -f vite`.

## RDKit
I read the [ai-expo-2026-code](https://github.com/potatoesandfrenchfries/ai-expo-2026-code) repo. Its only RDKit setup is a pinned `rdkit==2025.9.5` in `requirements.txt`. It uses RDKit for molecule filters (PAINS), descriptors, synthetic-accessibility scores and scaffold grouping. Those are useful later for the toxicity and drug-likeness filters.

I didn't copy that pin, because the worker already pins `rdkit==2026.9.1`. That version imports and works (I checked with aspirin's molecular weight). Pinning two versions in one environment would conflict.

`.devcontainer/post-create.sh` creates `$DOCKING_VENV` from

```bash
uv run deploy/db/migrate.py           # DATABASE_URL must be set

```

or the docking worker on its own:

```bash
OXHACK_REPO=postgres OXHACK_DOCKING=vina uv run python -m oxhack_worker.queue
```

Check one control by hand, without the database:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=worker "$DOCKING_VENV/bin/python" -m oxhack_worker.control 6WTO
```

On a Mac, run the docking venv side in an amd64 container (Docker Desktop with
"Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation" on):

```bash
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 -v "$PWD":/repo -w /repo -e PYTHONPATH=/repo/worker \
  python:3.11-slim-bookworm sh -c \
  'pip install -q -r .devcontainer/docking-requirements.txt && python -m oxhack_worker.control 6WTO'
```

### The whole stack on a Mac

Vina has no arm64 wheel, so on Apple Silicon the docking worker runs in an amd64
container (`oxhack-docking:local`, built from `.devcontainer/docking-requirements.txt`)
while the API runs natively. Both share the repository, so results land in
`data/docking/` for the API to serve. Use a local Postgres, not Tiger:

```bash
docker run -d --name oxhack-dockworker --platform linux/amd64 -v "$PWD":/repo -w /repo \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgresql://<user>:<password>@host.docker.internal:<port>/<db>" \
  -e OXHACK_REPO=postgres -e OXHACK_DOCKING=vina -e DOCKING_VENV=/usr/local \
  -e UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv -e UV_LINK_MODE=copy oxhack-docking:local \
  sh -c 'pip install -q uv && uv sync --all-packages --frozen --quiet &&
         exec uv run --no-sync python -m oxhack_worker.queue'
```

Then start the API with `OXHACK_REPO=postgres OXHACK_DOCKING=vina
DOCKING_VENV=/usr/local` and the same database on `127.0.0.1`.

## Which ligand is docked

The SMILES is fixed when a request is queued and saved with the job
(`dock_jobs.ligand_smiles`); the worker docks exactly that. The API takes it from
`api/oxhack_api/fixtures/docking.json` (hand-checked) or, for any other live
Candidate, from ChEMBL's parent record (`services/ligands.py`), kept in
`data/ligands/`. A drug ChEMBL does not call a small molecule (an antibody, a
protein) has no SMILES and is not offered for docking.

## Prepare the structures again

```bash
PYTHONPATH=worker "$DOCKING_VENV/bin/python" -m oxhack_worker.prepare   # or: ... prepare 6WTO
```

The set is the one in `api/oxhack_api/fixtures/structures.json`. Receptor
preparation keeps the docking chain's protein atoms and makes each residue match a
Meeko template without inventing coordinates:

- a residue whose side chain the crystal does not resolve is cut back to what it
  has (alanine when CB is there, else glycine);
- a phosphorylated residue far outside the box loses its phosphate (6WTO and
  6WTN: PTR 1007 and 1008, more than 20 angstroms from the box centre).

`meta.json` lists every change. Preparing again with another toolchain rewrites
`settings.json`; queued jobs then fail with a toolchain error, and new requests
and controls get new cache keys. Commit the results.

Vina 1.2.7, Meeko 0.8.0, RDKit 2026.09.1; exhaustiveness 8, seed 42, 9 poses, a
25 angstrom box on the crystal ligand. Measured on 25 October 2026 in an amd64
container under Rosetta on an Apple Silicon Mac (not yet in the codespace). Scores
and RMSDs did not change between 4 and 18 CPUs.

| 6WTN (JAK2) | ruxolitinib | -8.66 | 2.83 Å | failed | 1.42 Å (pose 3, -8.49) |
| 6O0K (BCL2) | venetoclax | -11.82 | 1.08 Å | passed | pose 1 |
| 7BQU (CRBN) | (S)-thalidomide | -9.39 | 0.41 Å | passed | pose 1 |

Both JAK2 controls fail the 2.0 angstrom threshold. In both top poses the
pyrrolopyrimidine hinge binder is turned: its pyrrole ring sits about 4 angstroms
from the crystal position and its pyrimidine about 1.7, while a near-native pose
